# m66 — 5×14 LEGO Ortholinear Keyboard
Status: Rev 4 Tested 5×14 Ortho (66 Keys) RP2040 Pro Micro / nice!nano / XIAO Per-Key RGB + Underglow OLED / Sharp / E-Ink / LCD QMK & ZMK
![m66 rev 4 LCD](pics/m66/mlego_m66_rev4-lcd.webp){ loading=lazy } ![m66 rev 4 Sharp Memory Display](pics/m66/mlego_m66_rev4-sharp.webp){ loading=lazy } ![m66 rev 4 Sharp Display](pics/m66/mlege-m66-rev4-sharp.webp){ loading=lazy }
The **m66** is a 5-row, 13-column ortholinear keyboard plus a dedicated clickable rotary encoder column (technically a 5×14 matrix), designed to accommodate all standard keycaps from an ISO layout. The current iteration (**Rev 4**) uses an **RP2040 Pro Micro–compatible footprint** (tested with Splinky, Helios, and `nice!nano` BLE boards), chained per-key RGB LEDs and underglow backlight, a clickable rotary encoder, and multi-display support for I²C OLED, Sharp Memory display, WeAct SSD1680 e-ink, and ST7735 IPS LCD screens. > **Status: **Rev 4** Done and Tested** > * [x] Gerbers designed * [x] Firmware (QMK & ZMK) * [ ] Breadboard tested * [x] Gerbers printed * [x] Board tested > **Revision History** > * **m66 Rev 4** *(formerly m65 Rev 12)*: RP2040 Pro Micro pinout with 2× `74HC595` shift registers, OLED / LCD (`ST7735` tested) / Sharp Memory / e-ink (`SSD1680` WeAct), clickable encoder, per-key RGB, and RGB backlight * **m66 Rev 3** *(formerly m65 Rev 11)*: XIAO RP2040 with 3 shift registers (2× `74HC595` + 1× `74HC589`), OLED / e-ink (`SSD1680` WeAct), and push rotary encoder with QMK (ZMK support in progress for RP2040 and nRF52840) * **m66 Rev 2** *(formerly m65 Rev 10)*: XIAO RP2040 with 3 shift registers (2× `74HC595` + 1× `74HC589`), OLED, and push rotary encoder with QMK * **m66 Rev 1** *(formerly m65 Rev 9)*: XIAO RP2040 with 3 shift registers (2× `74HC595` + 1× `74HC165`), OLED, and push rotary encoder with QMK * **m65 Rev 7/8**: XIAO RP2040 and nRF52840 with 2× `74HC595` shift registers, rotary encoder, no OLED (both QMK and ZMK firmware on RP2040) * **m65 Rev 5/6**: RP2040 support (Raspberry Pi Pico, WeAct, and compatible clones), non-push encoder, OLED * **m65 Rev 4**: `STM32F401`/`F411`, non-push encoder, OLED * **m65 Rev 3**: `STM32F401`/`F411`, non-push encoder * **m65 Rev 2**: `GD32F303` (BluePill Plus, USB-C F103 equivalent — ) * **m65 Rev 1**: `STM32F103` / `APM32F103` or `STM32F303` ## BOM { #bom } > **Microcontroller Notes (MCUs)** > I have used several reference MCU boards over time. Reference boards simplify DIY keyboard design since all high-frequency crystal and power circuitry is already on the module. While I have done handwire projects with AVR (`ATmega32U4`), I strongly advise against using them for new builds. * **m65 Rev 1**: `STM32F103` [BluePill](https://stm32-base.org/boards/STM32F103C8T6-Blue-Pill.html) or [RobotDyn `STM32F303CCT6` BlackPill](https://stm32-base.org/boards/STM32F303CCT6-RobotDyn-Black-Pill.html) *(do not confuse with the WeAct F401/F411 BlackPill)*. Micro-USB; requires flashing an `stm32duino` bootloader. * **m65 Rev 2**: `GD32F303` [BluePill Plus](https://github.com/WeActStudio/BluePill-Plus) with USB Type-C. * **m65 Rev 3/4**: WeAct [`STM32F401`/`F411` MiniF4x BlackPill](https://github.com/WeActStudio/WeActStudio.MiniSTM32F4x) with USB Type-C. * **m65 Rev 5/6**: `RP2040` ([Raspberry Pi Pico](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/microcontrollers/raspberry-pi-pico.html), [Waveshare RP2040-Plus](https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/RP2040-Plus), or USB-C compatible clones with matching pinouts). * **m65 Rev 7 / m66 Rev 1–3**: [Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040](https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO-RP2040/) and [XIAO BLE nRF52840](https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO_BLE/). Compact 14-pin footprint paired with SPI shift registers. * **m66 Rev 4**: `RP2040` in Pro Micro footprint (tested with **Splinky** and **Helios** pinouts) as well as **`nice!nano`** BLE controllers and clones. * **More pins**: If you need more direct GPIO pins in a compact package, check the [WeAct `STM32G431` CoreBoard](https://github.com/WeActStudio/WeActStudio.STM32G431CoreBoard) (supported in QMK). ### Rev 4 > **Revision 4 BOM** > * **MCU**: `RP2040` Pro Micro–compatible pinout (tested with Splinky and Helios-like MCUs) or `nice!nano` BLE MCUs * **Shift Registers**: 2× `74HC595` (SOIC-16 surface mount) * **Diodes**: 66× `1N4148` signal diodes (DO-35 through-hole or SOD-123 SMD) * **Display (optional)**: I²C OLED (128×32), Sharp Memory Display, ST7735 IPS LCD, or WeAct SSD1680 e-ink module * **Encoder**: Clickable EC11 rotary encoder (e.g., Bourns 24-pulse incremental mechanical encoder with 6 mm flat shaft) * **RGB (optional)**: Per-key SK6812 MINI-E LEDs and/or underglow RGB chain * **LEGO Enclosure**: 16×32 double-sided baseplate (or 2× 16×16 plates) + ~46× 1×2 or 1×4 LEGO plates/bricks ### Rev 3 ??? info "Revision 3 BOM (formerly m65 Rev 11)" * **LEGO**: ~46× 1×2 or 1×4 plates (or bricks if housing a LiPo battery), 1× 16×32 double-sided baseplate (or 2× 16×16 plates; gray plates minimize PCB bow), optional 4× 1×1 tiles/eyes and 4× 2×2 corner plates * **Diodes**: 66× `1N4148` signal diodes (DO-35 or SOD-123) * **Resistors**: 5× 10 kΩ (THT or SMD 1206) and 1× 5.1 kΩ (THT or SMD 1206) * **MCU**: Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040 (or XIAO nRF52840) with recommended female header sockets * **Shift Registers**: 2× `74HC595` (SOIC-16 SMD) and 1× `74HC589` (SOIC-16 SMD) * **Transistor**: 1× `2N7002` N-channel MOSFET (SOT-23 SMD) * **Capacitors (optional)**: 3× 100 nF decoupling capacitors * **Power / Battery (optional)**: Pogo pins, LiPo battery, 2-pin PH 2.0 battery connector, and 1P2T 4 mm micro slide switch * **Encoder**: Clickable EC11 rotary encoder (Bourns 24-pulse, 6 mm flat shaft) * **Display (optional)**: 128×32 I²C OLED (1×4 socket) or WeAct SSD1680 e-ink display (2×4 header/socket) ### Rev 2 ??? warning "Revision 2 BOM — Superseded by Rev 3 (formerly m65 Rev 10)" * Same component list as **Rev 3**, supporting I²C OLED (128×32) with 1×4 DIL socket (prior to the dedicated e-ink header addition in Rev 3). ### Rev 1 ??? info "Revision 1 BOM (formerly m65 Rev 9)" * **LEGO**: 16×32 double-sided plate (or 2× 16×16) + ~46× 1×2 or 1×4 plates * **Diodes**: 66× `1N4148` signal diodes (DO-35 or SOD-123) * **Resistors**: 5× 10 kΩ THT resistors * **MCU**: Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040 (or XIAO nRF52840) * **Shift Registers**: 2× `74HC595` (DIP-16 THT + sockets) and 1× `74HC165` (DIP-16 THT + socket) * **Capacitors (optional)**: 3× 100 nF decoupling capacitors (or integrated capacitor DIP sockets) * **Encoder & Battery**: EC11 clickable rotary encoder, optional LiPo battery + PH 2.0 socket + 1P2T switch ## Case & Enclosure { #case }
![Case 3D render](pics/m65-case.webp){ loading=lazy } ![LEGO parts for case](pics/lego_1.webp){ loading=lazy } ![Case front view](pics/lego_2.webp){ loading=lazy } ![Case back view](pics/lego_3.webp){ loading=lazy } ![Case side profile](pics/lego_4.webp){ loading=lazy }
## Assembly { #assembly } See the step-by-step [Assembly Guide](#doc/assembly) for soldering diodes, socketing the MCU and display, and mounting the PCB onto the LEGO baseplate. ## Thickness Profiles { #thickness } Depending on your LEGO plate stack, the enclosure can be built ultra-low-profile or tall enough to house underglow strips and batteries:
- ![8 mm thickness profile](pics/thick-1.webp){ loading=lazy } **8.0 mm — Ultra-Thin Profile** 1× double-sided baseplate + 1× intermediate plate (3.2 mm) + PCB (1.6 mm). Leaves room for a thin sheet of acoustic dampening foam. - ![11.2 mm thickness profile](pics/thick-2.webp){ loading=lazy } **11.2 mm — Mid Profile** 1× double-sided baseplate + 2× intermediate plates + PCB. Fits thicker foam or a direct-wired LED strip without a JST connector. - ![14.4 mm thickness profile](pics/thick-3.webp){ loading=lazy } **14.4 mm — Full Brick Profile** 1× double-sided baseplate + 1× full LEGO brick + PCB. Accommodates a 3-pin JST header or LiPo battery.

m65.markdown:
# m65 — 5×13 LEGO Ortholinear Keyboard
Status: Rev 11 Tested 5×13 Ortho (65–66 Keys) XIAO RP2040 / BLE · Pico · STM32 SPI Shift Registers (74HC595 / 589 / 165) OLED & E-Ink + Rotary Encoder QMK & ZMK
![m65 rev 11 with WeAct e-ink display](pics/mlego_m65_rev11_eink.webp){ loading=lazy } ![m65 rev 11 with OLED display](pics/mlego_m65_rev11_oled.webp){ loading=lazy }
The **m65** is a 5-row, 13-column ortholinear mechanical keyboard designed to accommodate all standard keycaps from an ISO layout. In its later iterations (**Rev 7–Rev 11**), it departs from a traditional direct-pin matrix and uses the tiny [Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040](https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO-RP2040/) or [Seeed Studio XIAO nRF52840 BLE](https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO_BLE/) (`SAMD21` may also work). Because the XIAO only exposes 11 GPIO pins, rows are scanned via a `74HC589` (or `74HC165`) input shift register while columns are driven by two chained `74HC595` output shift registers over hardware SPI (sharing clock and latch pins), leaving pins free for an I²C OLED / SPI e-ink screen and a clickable rotary encoder (making Rev 9–11 technically a 14-column matrix, later spun off into the [**m66**](#doc/m66) line). > **Seeed Studio Sponsorship** > For **Rev 7**, Seeed Studio kindly sponsored the 5×13 version with PCBs and XIAO microcontrollers as part of the [Seeed Fusion DIY XIAO Mechanical Keyboard Contest](https://www.seeedstudio.com/seeed-fusion-diy-xiao-mechanical-keyboard-contest.html) and their [Fusion PCB Assembly service](https://www.seeedstudio.com/pcb-assembly.html). > **Status: **Rev 11** Done and Tested** > * [x] Gerbers designed * [x] Firmware (QMK & ZMK) * [ ] Breadboard tested * [x] Gerbers printed * [x] Board tested > **Revision History** > * **Rev 11**: XIAO RP2040 with 3 shift registers (2× `74HC595` + 1× `74HC589`), OLED / e-ink (`SSD1680` WeAct), and push rotary encoder with QMK (actively exploring ZMK support for RP2040 and nRF52840) * **Rev 10**: XIAO RP2040 with 3 shift registers (2× `74HC595` + 1× `74HC589`), OLED, and push rotary encoder with QMK * **Rev 9**: XIAO RP2040 with 3 shift registers (2× `74HC595` + 1× `74HC165`), OLED, and push rotary encoder with QMK * **Rev 7/8**: XIAO RP2040 and nRF52840 with 2× `74HC595` shift registers, rotary encoder, no OLED (both QMK and ZMK firmware supported) * **Rev 5/6**: `RP2040` support (Raspberry Pi Pico, WeAct RP2040, and compatible clones), non-push encoder, OLED * **Rev 4**: `STM32F401`/`F411` BlackPill, non-push encoder, OLED * **Rev 3**: `STM32F401`/`F411` BlackPill, non-push encoder * **Rev 2**: `GD32F303` aka [BluePill Plus](https://github.com/WeActStudio/BluePill-Plus) (USB-C `F103` equivalent) * **Rev 1**: `STM32F103` / `APM32F103` or `STM32F303` ## BOM { #bom } ### Microcontrollers { #mcus } > **MCU Selection Guide** > Using off-the-shelf development boards makes DIY keyboard design much simpler because all high-frequency crystal and USB protection circuitry lives on the MCU daughterboard. While I have built handwired boards with AVR (`ATmega32U4`), I strongly advise against using AVR for new designs. * **Rev 1**: [`STM32F103C8T6` BluePill](https://stm32-base.org/boards/STM32F103C8T6-Blue-Pill.html) or [RobotDyn `STM32F303CCT6` BlackPill](https://stm32-base.org/boards/STM32F303CCT6-RobotDyn-Black-Pill.html) *(do not confuse with the WeAct F401/F411 BlackPill)*. Micro-USB; requires flashing an `stm32duino` bootloader. * **Rev 2**: `GD32F303` [BluePill Plus](https://github.com/WeActStudio/BluePill-Plus) with USB Type-C. * **Rev 3 / Rev 4**: WeAct [`STM32F401`/`F411` MiniSTM32F4x BlackPill](https://github.com/WeActStudio/WeActStudio.MiniSTM32F4x) with USB Type-C. * **Rev 5 / Rev 6**: `RP2040` ([Raspberry Pi Pico](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/microcontrollers/raspberry-pi-pico.html), [Waveshare RP2040-Plus](https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/RP2040-Plus), or USB-C compatible clones — verify pinout compatibility). * **Rev 7 / Rev 9 / Rev 10 / Rev 11**: [Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040](https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO-RP2040/) and [Seeed Studio XIAO BLE nRF52840](https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO_BLE/). Ultra-compact footprint using SPI shift registers for matrix scanning. * **Need more pins?**: Consider the [WeAct `STM32G431` CoreBoard](https://github.com/WeActStudio/WeActStudio.STM32G431CoreBoard), already supported in QMK. ### Component Lists by Revision #### Rev 11 > **Revision 11 BOM** > * **LEGO Case**: ~46× 1×2 or 1×4 plates (use full bricks if housing a battery), 1× 16×32 double-sided baseplate or 2× 16×16 plates (gray compatible plates minimize PCB flexing), optional 4× 1×1 tiles/eyes and 4× 2×2 corner plates * **Diodes**: 66× `1N4148` signal diodes (DO-35 through-hole or SOD-123 SMD) * **Resistors**: 5× 10 kΩ (THT or SMD 1206) and 1× 5.1 kΩ (THT or SMD 1206) * **MCU**: Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040 (or nRF52840) + recommended female socket headers * **Shift Registers**: 2× `74HC595` (SOIC-16 SMD) and 1× `74HC589` (SOIC-16 SMD) * **MOSFET**: 1× `2N7002` FET (SOT-23 SMD) * **Capacitors (optional)**: 3× 100 nF decoupling capacitors (THT, SMD, or integrated socket) * **Battery / Wireless (optional)**: Pogo pins, LiPo battery, 2-pin PH 2.0 battery socket, and 1P2T 4 mm micro slide switch * **Encoder**: Clickable EC11 rotary encoder (Bourns 24-pulse incremental encoder with 6 mm flat shaft) * **Displays (optional)**: * 128×32 I²C OLED (4-pin) + 1×4 DIL socket * WeAct SSD1680 e-ink module + 2×4 header and socket #### Rev 10 ??? QMK provides `OLED_UPDATE_INTERVAL` (in milliseconds) to throttle display refreshes. Tested on **Rev 9** (`128×32` and `128×64` screens yield identical numbers; baselines with OLED off: `3760 Hz` with WPM off, `2631 Hz` with WPM on): | `OLED_UPDATE_INTERVAL` [ms] | Matrix Scan Frequency [Hz] | | :---: | :---: | | `0` *(QMK default)* | `2125` | | `1` | `3154` | | `2` | `3629` | | `3` | `3788` | | `4` | `3868` | | `5` | `3915` | | **`10`** *(100 FPS — recommended)* | **`4011`** | | `20` | `4058` | | `30` | `4075` | | `50` | `4087` | | `100` | `4097` | > **Takeaways** > 1. Setting `OLED_UPDATE_INTERVAL` to **`10` ms** (100 FPS) nearly doubles the effective matrix scan rate (`4011 Hz` vs `2125 Hz`) while remaining more than fast enough for any keyboard status OLED. 2. Curiously, throttling the OLED refresh achieves a higher peak scan rate (`4097 Hz`) than compiling with the OLED disabled (`3760 Hz`).

# m60 — 5×12 LEGO Ortholinear Keyboard
Status: Rev 1 & Rev 2 Tested 5×12 Ortho (60 Keys) STM32F401 / RP2040 Pico Rotary Encoder + OLED (Rev 2) QMK (UF2)
![M60 5x12 rev 1](pics/5x12/m60.webp){ loading=lazy } ![M60 5x12 rev 2](pics/5x12/m60_rev2.webp){ loading=lazy }
A Preonic-inspired **5×12 ortholinear mechanical keyboard** mounted in a modular LEGO case, featuring an optional rotary encoder, RGB underglow strip, and I²C OLED support (Rev 2, thanks to `@yyhazy`). > **Status: Rev 1 & Rev 2 Tested** > * [x] Gerbers designed * [x] Firmware * [x] Breadboard tested * [x] Gerbers printed * [x] Board tested ## Features * **Layout**: 5×12 ortholinear (60 keys, 5-pin PCB-mount MX switches) * **Controller**: * **Rev 1**: WeAct [`STM32F401`/`F411` BlackPill](https://github.com/WeActTC/MiniSTM32F4x1) * **Rev 2**: Raspberry Pi Pico (`RP2040`) or compatible pinout * **Peripherals**: Optional EC11 rotary encoder, 3-pin addressable LED strip, and I²C OLED display (Rev 2) * **Firmware**: QMK with UF2 drag-and-drop flashing by default ## An ergonomic **5×12 split ortholinear keyboard** mounted on two 16×16 LEGO baseplates, featuring dual rotary encoders (one per half) and addressable RGB underglow. > **Status: Tested All OK** > * [x] Gerbers designed * [x] Firmware * [x] Breadboard tested * [x] Gerbers printed * [x] Board tested ## Features * **Layout**: 5×12 split (two 5×6 halves, 60 keys total) * **Controllers**: 2× WeAct [`STM32F401` (Rev 1) or `STM32F411` (Rev 2) BlackPill](https://github.com/WeActTC/MiniSTM32F4x1) * **Peripherals**: 1× rotary encoder per half, RGB underglow strip, 4× status LEDs * **Interconnect**: Direct 3-wire serial cable via angled 3-pin JST XH 2.54 mm connectors * **Firmware**: QMK with TinyUF2 bootloader support ## Renders & PCBs { #renders } === "Left & Right Printed PCBs" ![M60 split 5x12 left/right PCB](pics/5x12s/m60_split_pcb.webp){ loading=lazy } === "KiCad Left & Right Layout"

# SteelSeries Prime — QMK Mouse Liberation
Difficulty: Medium (Soldering + SWD) STM32F103C8T6 PixArt PMW3389 (TrueMove Pro) 6 Buttons + RGB Wheel UF2 Bootloader + QMK
![SteelSeries Prime mouse](pics/prime.webp){ loading=lazy } The wired [SteelSeries Prime](https://steelseries.com/gaming-mice/prime) is an affordable, lightweight gaming mouse (picked up from a local discounter, B&M, for £15) built around an **`STM32F103C8T6`** microcontroller, a **TrueMove Pro** optical sensor (compatible with QMK's PixArt `PMW3389` driver), 6 buttons, and an RGB scroll wheel LED. Because the fancier **Prime+** shares the same MCU and optical sensor and was already ported to QMK by **Dasky**, adapting the standard Prime was straightforward. Converting it requires opening the shell, soldering a 5-pin SWD header, unlocking flash protection via `openocd`, and flashing a UF2 bootloader. ## Internal PCBs { #pcbs }
![SteelSeries Prime PCB front](pics/prime_front.webp){ loading=lazy } ![SteelSeries Prime PCB back with lens removed](pics/prime_back.webp){ loading=lazy }
## Required Tools { #tools } * **Screwdrivers**: `PH0` (for internal PCB screws) and `TX6` Torx (for external case screws beneath the skates) * **SWD Programmer**: `ST-Link v2` (an inexpensive clone from RobotDyn/AliExpress works fine) * **Soldering Gear**: Soldering iron, 5-pin 2.54 mm pitch header strip, and 3–4 female-to-female DuPont jumper wires ## Teardown & Preparation { #prep } 1. **Remove PTFE Skates**: Carefully peel back the glued PTFE feet covering the bottom screws so they can be reused after reassembly (or keep replacement skates on hand). 2. **Open the Shell**: Unscrew the 4 external case screws using the `TX6` driver. 3. **Disconnect Ribbon Cable**: Gently separate the top shell and release the internal ribbon cable using its zero-insertion-force latch lever. 4. **Remove Internal PCB**: Unscrew the 2 main PCB screws plus the 2 additional screws next to the scroll wheel (`PH0`). Lift the PCB out of the lower housing (don't worry if the small plastic alignment prong on the side of the PCB snaps). 5. **Solder SWD Header**: Clear any factory solder from the 5 through-holes on the SWD header footprint and solder the 2.54 mm pin header in place. ## Flashing the UF2 Bootloader { #bootloader } 1. **Wire ST-Link to the Mouse PCB**: * If powering the mouse via its USB cable, connect 3 DuPont wires: `GND`, `SWCLK`, and `SWDIO`. * If powering directly from the ST-Link, connect a 4th wire for `VCC` (3.3 V). 2. **Download or Build the Bootloader**: * **Prebuilt Binary**: [ `firmware/uf2boot_prime.bin`](https://gitlab.com/m-lego/m65/-/blob/devel/firmware/uf2boot_prime.bin) * **Build from Source**: Clone [`daskygit/uf2-prime-plus`](https://github.com/daskygit/uf2-prime-plus), apply the patch below to rename the USB volume/product labels for the standard Prime, and build target `PRIME_PLUS`: ```diff diff --git a/libopencm3/Makefile b/libopencm3/Makefile index d93efeac..d5c2e4d6 100644 --- a/libopencm3/Makefile +++ b/libopencm3/Makefile @@ -59,7 +59,7 @@ build: lib LIB_DIRS:=$(wildcard $(addprefix lib/,$(TARGETS))) $(LIB_DIRS): $(IRQ_DEFN_FILES:=.genhdr) @printf " BUILD $@\n"; - $(Q)$(MAKE) --directory=$@ SRCLIBDIR="$(SRCLIBDIR)" + $(Q)$(MAKE) --directory=$@ SRCLIBDIR=$(SRCLIBDIR) lib: $(LIB_DIRS) $(Q)true diff --git a/src/stm32f103/prime_plus/config.h b/src/stm32f103/prime_plus/config.h index d7c2b50..6fe0eb7 100644 --- a/src/stm32f103/prime_plus/config.h +++ b/src/stm32f103/prime_plus/config.h @@ -49,11 +49,11 @@ #define UF2_FAMILY 0x5ee21072 #undef VOLUME_LABEL -#define VOLUME_LABEL "PRIMEPLUS" +#define VOLUME_LABEL "PRIME" #undef PRODUCT_NAME -#define PRODUCT_NAME "SteelSeries Prime+" +#define PRODUCT_NAME "SteelSeries Prime" #undef BOARD_ID -#define BOARD_ID "steelseries-prime-plus" +#define BOARD_ID "steelseries-prime" ``` 3. **Remove `STM32F103` Write Protection**: Using `openocd` (or STM32CubeProgrammer): ```sh openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f1x.cfg \ -c "init; reset halt; stm32f1x unlock 0; flash protect 0 0 last off; reset halt; exit" ``` 4. **Flash the UF2 Bootloader**: ```sh openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f1x.cfg \ -c "program uf2boot.bin verify reset exit 0x8000000" ``` 5. **Reassemble**: Disconnect power and remove the ST-Link jumper wires, then reassemble the PCB, ribbon cable, shell, and skates. ## QMK Firmware { #firmware } 1. **Enter UF2 Bootloader Mode**: Hold down the **underside CPI button** while plugging in the USB cable. A removable USB mass-storage drive (`PRIME`) will mount on your computer. 2. **Flash QMK**: * **Prebuilt UF2**: Download [ `firmware/steelseries_prime_default.uf2`](https://gitlab.com/m-lego/m65/-/blob/devel/firmware/steelseries_prime_default.uf2) and copy it onto the mounted drive. * **Compile from Source**: ```bash git clone --recurse-submodules -b mlego_dev https://github.com/alinelena/qmk_firmware.git qmk-alin cd qmk-alin qmk compile -kb steelseries/prime -km default qmk flash -kb steelseries/prime -km default ```

# Not Enough Pins for Your Keyboard Matrix?
SPI Shift Registers 74HC595 · 74HC165 · 74HC589 Matrix Remapping (5×13 → 8×9) QMK & ZMK
So you decided to wire a custom mechanical keyboard, but your favorite compact microcontroller doesn't expose enough GPIO pins for the full switch matrix. This is the exact challenge I hit when moving the 65-key [**m65**](#doc/m65) onto the tiny 11-pin **Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040**. ## Common Pin-Reduction Approaches Before settling on SPI shift registers, I surveyed the existing approaches used in the community: * **Duplex Matrix**: Folds long rows/columns by wiring two switches per row/column intersection with opposing diodes. Effective, but makes schematic reading and routing more mentally taxing. * **Direct-Pin Shift Registers**: Used in boards like [tzarc's Ghoul](https://github.com/tzarc/ghoul) with chained `74HC589` shift registers (one bit per switch, no matrix). Great scan speed, but requires many ICs for 65+ keys. * **I²C IO Expanders & Demuxers**: Popular on split boards (e.g., [Ferris IO Expander guide](https://github.com/pierrechevalier83/ferris/wiki/Understanding-the-QMK-firmware-for-the-IO-Expander)) or `74HC138` 3-to-8 decoders in QMK. * **SPI Shift-Register Matrix Scanning**: Using inexpensive `74HC595` (serial-in, parallel-out) and `74HC165` / `74HC589` (parallel-in, serial-out) shift registers to drive columns and/or read rows over hardware SPI. * Background tutorials on shift registers: [Last Minute Engineers — `74HC595`](https://lastminuteengineers.com/74hc595-shift-register-arduino-tutorial/) and [DroneBot Workshop — `74HC595` & `74HC165`](https://dronebotworkshop.com/shift-registers/). * Initial keyboard inspiration: [mehmedbasic.dk — `74HC595` Keyboard](https://mehmedbasic.dk/post/74hc595-keyboard/). > **Official QMK Support & Acknowledgments** > When I started experimenting with these circuits, QMK had very few public examples. Since QMK `0.20.0`, boards like Keychron and `hazel/bad_wings` use `74HC595`, and `handwired/dqz11n1g` uses `74HC165`. Huge thanks to **sigprof** and **tzarc** for their guidance on SPI timing and tri-state buffering. > **Disclaimer** > While the schematics and firmware below work reliably together to scan a 13×5 / 14×5 matrix at 4,000–6,000+ Hz, remember I am a hardware enthusiast rather than an electrical engineer — use and adapt them at your own risk! --- ## Method 1: Scan Columns via `74HC595` + Direct GPIO Rows { #1-scan-only-columns-with-shift-registers } Uses **2× [`74HC595`](https://www.ti.com/product/SN74HC595)** output shift registers chained over SPI (`MOSI`, `SCK`, `RCLK`) to drive up to 16 columns using only **3 MCU pins**, while the 5 rows are read directly on 5 MCU GPIO pins (total: **8 pins** for a 5×16 matrix). ![Matrix Version 1 — 2x 74HC595 column scanning](pics/matrix-1.webp){ loading=lazy } * **QMK Implementation**: [`mlego/m65/rev7/matrix.c`](https://github.com/alinelena/qmk_firmware/tree/mlego_dev/keyboards/mlego/m65/rev7/matrix.c) * **ZMK Implementation**: [`mlego5x13_rev8.overlay` (`zmk,kscan-gpio-matrix` + `74hc595`)](https://github.com/alinelena/mlego-zmk/blob/main/config/boards/shields/mlego5x13_rev8/mlego5x13_rev8.overlay) --- ## Method 2a: Scan Columns (`74HC595`) & Rows (`74HC165`) — Unbuffered { #2a-scan-both-columns-and-rows-with-shift-registers } Uses **2× `74HC595`** (columns) and **1× [`74HC165`](https://www.ti.com/product/SN74HC165)** (rows). Both ICs are inexpensive and widely available in through-hole (DIP-16) and SMD (SOIC-16) packages. Reads the entire 5×14 matrix using only **4 MCU pins** (`MOSI`, `MISO`, `SCK`, shared `Latch`). > **Limitation: Unbuffered `MISO`** > Because the `74HC165` serial output (`Q7`) does not have a true high-impedance (3-state) output when deselected, **you cannot easily share the `MISO` pin with other SPI peripherals** without adding external tri-state buffer circuitry. ![Matrix Version 2a — 2x 74HC595 + 1x 74HC165](pics/matrix-2a.webp){ loading=lazy } * **QMK Implementation**: [`mlego/m66/rev1/matrix.c`](https://github.com/alinelena/qmk_firmware/blob/mlego_dev/keyboards/mlego/m66/rev1/matrix.c) --- ## Method 2b: Scan Columns (`74HC595`) & Rows (`74HC589`) — Buffered 3-State SPI { #2b-scan-both-columns-and-rows-with-shift-registers } Replaces the `74HC165` with a **1× [`74HC589`](https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/mc74hc589a-d.pdf)** (mostly SMD today). The `74HC589` includes an internal **3-state output buffer**, allowing the `MISO` line to be cleanly shared with other SPI devices (such as SPI e-ink or Sharp Memory displays). ### Variant 1 (Single Shared Latch — Deprecated) { #variant-1 } > **Do Not Use Variant 1 for New Designs** > While this single-latch circuit (`m65 Rev 10` / `m66 Rev 2`) works with carefully tuned firmware timing, it relies on edge-case latch/output-enable behavior. Use **Variant 2** below instead. ![Matrix Version 2b Variant 1](pics/matrix-2b.webp){ loading=lazy } * **QMK Reference**: [`mlego/m66/rev2/matrix.c`](https://github.com/alinelena/qmk_firmware/blob/mlego_dev/keyboards/mlego/m66/rev2/matrix.c) ### Variant 2 (Separate Chip Selects — Recommended) { #variant-2 } Uses separate latch / chip-select lines for the `2× 74HC595` column driver and the `1× 74HC589` row reader (costing 1 extra pin compared to Variant 1, for **5 SPI pins total**), making SPI bus sharing and matrix scanning clean and deterministic. ![Matrix Version 2b Variant 2](pics/matrix-2b_v2.webp){ loading=lazy } * **QMK Implementation**: [`mlego/m66/rev3/matrix.c`](https://github.com/alinelena/qmk_firmware/blob/mlego_dev/keyboards/m66/rev3/matrix.c) > **Hybrid Scanning** > All three shift-register methods above can be combined with direct GPIO pins in custom `matrix.c` routines if you want to mix shift-register columns with extra direct keys. --- ## Method 3: Mathematical Matrix Restructuring (Zero Extra Hardware) { #restructure-the-matrix } If you are only short by **1 or 2 GPIO pins**, you don't need any shift registers at all — simply **decouple the electrical matrix dimensions from the physical key layout** so the row and column counts are closer to a square (Rows ≈ Cols maximizes Rows × Cols for a fixed pin budget Rows + Cols). * **Example 1**: A physical **6×17** board (68 keys) normally requires 6 + 17 = 23 pins. Electrically wiring it as a **10×7** or **9×8** matrix reduces the pin count to 17 pins — saving **6 pins**! * **Example 2 (`m65` 5×13 Ortho)**: * **Standard 5×13 Matrix**: Uses 5 + 13 = **18 pins** (`65` positions). * **Restructured 8×9 Matrix**: Uses 8 + 9 = **17 pins** (`72` positions, saving 1 pin with 7 spare switch slots!). Both QMK (via data-driven `info.json` `"matrix": [row, col]` coordinates) and ZMK (via `zmk,matrix-transform`) make this remapping trivial: === "Standard 5×13 Matrix (18 Pins)" **1. `info.json` Pin Definition (`5 + 13 = 18` pins)**: ```json "matrix_pins": { "cols": ["GP1", "GP6", "GP7", "GP8", "GP9", "GP15", "GP14", "GP13", "GP12", "GP11", "GP10", "GP17", "GP21"], "rows": ["GP22", "GP16", "GP18", "GP19", "GP20"] } ``` **2. # How a Keyboard Matrix Works — Practical 3×3 Guide
COL2ROW vs. ROW2COL QMK Data-Driven Config STM32F401 & RP2040 KiCad PCB Design
## Setting Up the Scene { #set-up-the-scene } If you have read the official QMK guides — [How a Keyboard Matrix Works](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/how_a_matrix_works), [How Keyboards Work](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/how_keyboards_work), and [Understanding QMK's Code](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/understanding_qmk) — and want a concrete, end-to-end example connecting the schematic, diode orientation, QMK firmware, and PCB layout, this guide walks through a complete **3×3 mechanical keypad (`m3x3`)** using a WeAct **`STM32F401` BlackPill** (and **Raspberry Pi Pico `RP2040`**). > **MCU Pin Quirks** > Every microcontroller family has its own pin constraints and boot strapping requirements. Always check which pins are reserved or require pull-ups before finalizing a PCB: * [WeAct BlackPill `STM32F401CCU6` Pinout](https://stm32-base.org/boards/STM32F401CCU6-WeAct-Black-Pill-V1.2.html) & [`STM32F411CEU6` Pinout](https://stm32-base.org/boards/STM32F411CEU6-WeAct-Black-Pill-V2.0.html) * [QMK WeAct BlackPill `STM32F4x1` Platform Notes](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/platformdev_blackpill_f4x1?id=weact-blackpill-stm32f4x1) ### Diode Orientation: `COL2ROW` vs. `ROW2COL` Adding a `1N4148` signal diode in series with each key switch prevents **ghosting** when multiple keys are pressed simultaneously. Because a diode conducts current in only one direction, there are two valid ways to orient the diodes across your matrix intersections: | `COL2ROW` (Column → Row) | `ROW2COL` (Row → Column) | | :---: | :---: | | ![circuit schematic diode orientation columns to rows](pics/col2row/circuit-col2row.webp){ loading=lazy } | ![circuit schematic diode orientation rows to columns](pics/row2col/circuit-row2col.webp){ loading=lazy } | | Diode cathode (black band) points toward the **Row** line | Diode cathode (black band) points toward the **Column** line | In both circuits above, **Rows (`R0–R2`)** connect to `B3`, `B4`, `B5` and **Columns (`C0–C2`)** connect to `B12`, `B13`, `B14`. The only hardware difference is the direction of the diode! In QMK's `config.h` (or `info.json`), this is configured via `DIODE_DIRECTION`: === "Left Circuit (`COL2ROW`)" ```c // config.h #define DIODE_DIRECTION COL2ROW ``` ```json // info.json "diode_direction": "COL2ROW" ``` === "Right Circuit (`ROW2COL`)" ```c // config.h #define DIODE_DIRECTION ROW2COL ``` ```json // info.json "diode_direction": "ROW2COL" ``` At this stage, you already have everything needed to write and test the firmware on a breadboard using only the MCU and a few DuPont jumper wires! --- ## Creating a Simple QMK Firmware { #creating-a-simple-firmware } Once you have [set up your QMK environment](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/newbs_getting_started), QMK's CLI can scaffold the entire keyboard definition automatically. > **Design Parameters for `m3x3`** > * **MCU Type**: `blackpill_f401` (or `blackpill_f411`) * **Column Pins (`C0–C2`)**: `B12`, `B13`, `B14` *(order matters!)* * **Row Pins (`R0–R2`)**: `B3`, `B4`, `B5` *(order matters!)* * **Diode Direction**: `COL2ROW` * **Keyboard Name**: `m3x3` * **GitHub Username / Author**: `alinelena` / `"dr faustroll"` ### Scaffold the Keyboard ```bash qmk new-keyboard -n "dr faustroll" -u alinelena -t blackpill_f401 -kb m3x3 -l ortho_3x3 ``` QMK generates the following directory structure inside `keyboards/m3x3/`: ```text Ψ Generating a new QMK keyboard directory Ψ Created a new keyboard called m3x3. Ψ To start working on things, `cd` into keyboards/m3x3, Ψ or open the directory in your preferred text editor. Ψ And build with qmk compile -kb m3x3 -km default. keyboards/m3x3/ ├── config.h ├── info.json ├── keymaps/ │ └── default/ │ └── keymap.c ├── readme.md └── rules.mk ``` ### Configure `info.json` and `keymap.c` 1. **Set Diode Direction (`keyboards/m3x3/info.json`)**: ```json "diode_direction": "COL2ROW", ``` 2. **Set Matrix Pins (`keyboards/m3x3/info.json`)**: Replace the placeholder pins with our actual row and column pins: ```json "matrix_pins": { "cols": ["B12", "B13", "B14"], "rows": ["B3", "B4", "B5"] }, ``` 3. **Customize the Keymap (`keyboards/m3x3/keymaps/default/keymap.c`)**: See QMK's [Basic Keycodes reference](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/keycodes_basic). Replace the default `KC_A`–`KC_I` block with a 1–9 numpad layout: ```c [0] = LAYOUT_ortho_3x3( KC_7, KC_8, KC_9, KC_4, KC_5, KC_6, KC_1, KC_2, KC_3 ) ``` 4. **Compile & Flash**: ```bash qmk compile -kb m3x3 -km default qmk flash -kb m3x3 -km default ``` ```text Linking: .build/m3x3_default.elf [OK] Creating binary load file for flashing: .build/m3x3_default.bin [OK] Size after: text data bss dec hex filename 0 23032 0 23032 59f8 m3x3_default.bin ``` --- ## What If My Layout Is Not Listed in `qmk new-keyboard`? { #my-layout-is-not-listed } If your exact matrix dimensions aren't listed as a community layout preset, simply bootstrap with the closest larger preset (for example, `ortho_4x4`) and trim `keyboards/m3x3/info.json` and `keymaps/default/keymap.c`: 1. Update `"diode_direction"` and `"matrix_pins"` in `keyboards/m3x3/info.json` to 3 columns and 3 rows as shown above. 2. In `keyboards/m3x3/info.json`, rename `"LAYOUT_ortho_4x4"` to `"LAYOUT_ortho_3x3"` and remove any entries referencing row `3` or column `3`: ```json "LAYOUT_ortho_3x3": { "layout": [ { "matrix": [0, 0], "x": 0, "y": 0 }, { "matrix": [0, 1], "x": 1, "y": 0 }, { "matrix": [0, 2], "x": 2, "y": 0 }, { "matrix": [1, 0], "x": 0, "y": 1 }, { "matrix": [1, 1], "x": 1, "y": 1 }, { "matrix": [1, 2], "x": 2, "y": 1 }, { "matrix": [2, 0], "x": 0, "y": 2 }, { "matrix": [2, 1], "x": 1, "y": 2 }, { "matrix": [2, 2], "x": 2, "y": 2 } ] } ``` 3. Update `keyboards/m3x3/keymaps/default/keymap.c` to use `LAYOUT_ortho_3x3` with 9 keys, then compile and flash! --- ## Using Raspberry Pi Pico (`RP2040`) { #i-want-to-use-raspberry-pico-rp2040 } Switching to an `RP2040` board is just a matter of choosing `-t RP2040` and specifying valid `GPx` pin names: * [Official Raspberry Pi Pico Pinout PDF](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/pico/Pico-R3-A4-Pinout.pdf) *(always verify the pinout diagram for your specific RP2040 clone)* * [QMK `RP2040` Platform Documentation](https://docs.qmk.fm/#/platformdev_rp2040) ```bash qmk new-keyboard -n "dr faustroll" -u alinelena -t RP2040 -kb m3x3 -l ortho_3x3 ``` Then set your chosen GPIO pins (for example, `GP0`–`GP2` for columns and `GP10`–`GP12` for rows) in `keyboards/m3x3/info.json`: ```json "diode_direction": "COL2ROW", "matrix_pins": { "cols": ["GP0", "GP1", "GP2"], "rows": ["GP10", "GP11", "GP12"] }, ``` --- ## Designing the PCB in KiCad { #pcbs } Once your firmware is tested, you can either [handwire the switches](#doc/hand5x5) or design a custom PCB in **KiCad**: * **PCB Design Tutorial**: [ai03's Keyboard PCB Design Guide](https://wiki.ai03.com/books/pcb-design) * **KiCad Footprints & Symbols**: [ebastler's `marbastlib`](https://github.com/ebastler/marbastlib) and [mechkey.org resources](https://mechkey.org/) ### Side-by-Side PCB Comparison (`COL2ROW` vs. `ROW2COL`) | View | `COL2ROW` (Column → Row) | `ROW2COL` (Row → Column) | | :--- | :---: | :---: | | **KiCad Routed Tracks** | ![PCB tracks COL2ROW](pics/col2row/pcb-col2row.webp){ loading=lazy } | ![PCB tracks ROW2COL](pics/row2col/pcb-row2col.webp){ loading=lazy } | | **3D Render (Front)** | ![PCB 3D front COL2ROW](pics/col2row/pcb-3df-col2row.webp){ loading=lazy } | ![PCB 3D front ROW2COL](pics/row2col/pcb-3df-row2col.webp){ loading=lazy } | | **3D Render (Bottom)** | ![PCB 3D bottom COL2ROW](pics/col2row/pcb-3db-col2row.webp){ loading=lazy } | ![PCB 3D bottom ROW2COL](pics/row2col/pcb-3db-row2col.webp){ loading=lazy } |

# mlego — Modular LEGO Ortholinear Keyboards Custom ISO-friendly ortholinear mechanical keyboards, macropads, POS terminal conversions, and QMK/ZMK firmware experiments — all mounted in modular LEGO cases.
[Explore Keyboards ](#doc/home){ .md-button .md-button--primary } [Assembly Guide ](#doc/assembly){ .md-button } [GitLab Repository ](https://gitlab.com/m-lego/m65){ .md-button }
![mlego keyboard collection](pics/keybs.webp){ loading=lazy }
- { .lg .middle } **What This Project Is** --- * **Fun & experimental** — designed for learning electronics, PCB routing, and firmware * **Educational** — documented schematics, shift-register matrices, and QMK/ZMK configs * **Functional daily drivers** — full ISO keycap compatibility on compact ortho grids * **Budget-friendly** — cheap PCBs and LEGO plate enclosures (until switches & MT3 keycaps!) - { .lg .middle } **What This Project Is Not** --- * **Not "endgame"** — this is an evolving maker playground rather than a commercial CNC custom kit * Every revision explores a new microcontroller, display technology (OLED, e-ink, Sharp Memory, IPS LCD), or matrix scanning circuit
## Explore the Collection
- ![m65 and m66 family](pics/m65-rev1-10.webp){ loading=lazy } ** [Designed Keyboards](#doc/home)** --- From the flagship **m66** (5×14 with RGB & multi-screen support) and **m65** (5×13 ortho) to the **m60**, **m60 Split**, **m48**, and compact macropads (**m20**, **m8**, **m4**). [ Browse 8 keyboard models](#doc/home) - ![Converted Tipro POS terminals](pics/converted-all.webp){ loading=lazy } ** [Converted POS Keyboards](#doc/home)** --- Vintage mechanical **Tipro** point-of-sale terminals rescued from eBay, stripped, repainted, and liberated with custom STM32 daughterboards running QMK. [ View 5 Tipro conversions](#doc/home) - ![SteelSeries Prime mouse](pics/prime.webp){ loading=lazy } ** [QMK Mice](#doc/home)** --- Hardware bootloader unlocking and QMK firmware liberation for the **SteelSeries Prime** gaming mouse (`STM32F103` + `PMW3389` sensor). [ Read the Prime conversion guide](#doc/prime) - ![Matrix shift register schematic](pics/matrix-2b_v2.webp){ loading=lazy } ** [Hardware & Firmware Guides](#doc/home)** --- Step-by-step soldering & LEGO case assembly, SPI shift-register matrix scanning (`74HC595` / `74HC165` / `74HC589`), QMK matrix remapping, and modular 5×5 handwire PCBs. [ Explore engineering notes](#doc/home)
## Motivation & Background This project started as a fun exploration into building an **ISO-friendly ortholinear keyboard**. Initially conceived as a 6×13 grid, it settled into a **5×13** (and **5×14** with a dedicated rotary encoder column) layout as the sweet spot between compactness and standard ISO keycap compatibility. Read the original story on [Alin's blog](https://alin.elena.re/#post/keeblego). If you are exploring similar ortholinear ecosystems, check out the [6×13 Index-Tab](https://github.com/Kyrremann/index-tab), [4×13 Nack](https://github.com/farfalleflickan/nack), [mechkey.org](https://mechkey.org/), and [mechdb.net](https://mechdb.net/). ## What Makes mlego Keyboards Special? * **Modular LEGO Case**: PCBs are drilled to official LEGO stud pitch and thickness (1.6 mm), snapping directly onto LEGO plates and bricks for customizable height, tilt angle, and colors. * **Accessible Reference MCUs**: Built around off-the-shelf development boards — `STM32F103` / `GD32F303` BluePill, WeAct `STM32F401`/`F411` BlackPill, `STM32G431`, Raspberry Pi Pico (`RP2040`), Pro Micro `RP2040` (Splinky/Helios), `nice!nano`, and Seeed Studio `XIAO RP2040` / `XIAO nRF52840 BLE`. * **Shift-Register Matrix Scanning**: Later revisions pack full 65–66 key matrices + displays + encoders onto tiny 11-pin XIAO controllers using chained `74HC595`, `74HC165`, and buffered `74HC589` SPI shift registers. * **Rich Peripherals**: Clickable EC11 rotary encoders, per-key and underglow RGB LEDs, 128×32 I²C OLEDs, WeAct SSD1680 e-ink displays, Sharp Memory displays, and ST7735 IPS LCDs. ## Builder Tips & LEGO Tolerances > **LEGO Dimensional Tolerances** > PCB mounting holes are drilled to official LEGO stud dimensions. However, both PCB CNC drills and LEGO injection molds have manufacturing tolerances — and **LEGO clutch power varies slightly by plastic color**. * Use **1×2 and 1×4 plates** along the perimeter for the best fit. Longer plates can exert surprising force and slightly bow the PCB. * For the 16×32 double-sided baseplate (or two 16×16 plates), gray compatible baseplates tend to sit flattest without flexing the PCB. > **Typing Angle vs. Low-Profile Flat Base** > If you prefer a zero-degree flat typing profile, use a single-sided baseplate with one intermediate plate layer (total thickness ≈ 8 mm). For a ~6° typing angle, stack a full LEGO brick + plate along the rear edge. > **Acoustic Foam Dampening** > Lining the bottom cavity of the LEGO case with inexpensive A4 hobbycraft EVA/neoprene foam sheets makes a dramatic improvement to typing acoustics and eliminates hollow plastic resonance.
